content:
Moving keyboard shortcuts to a programmable macro keyboard is the most effective productivity improvement I've ever made.

Keyboard Shortcut Discovery Journey

I first encountered keyboard shortcuts through macOS's simple text replacement feature—using @@ for my primary email address, then using similar shortcuts to enter my full name, address, phone number, zip code, and so on.

Then I decided to level up by setting up shortcuts through Keyboard Maestro to directly open my most-used folders and applications.

From Desktop to Downloads to work-related folders, pressing Fn+F1 through Fn+F6 has become pure muscle memory, taking me where it used to take several mouse clicks to reach. The other function keys are used to launch my frequently used apps and websites, as well as Keyboard Maestro's clipboard history switcher.

Then I started automating my workflow further, including opening QuickTime and starting a new recording, as well as automatically launching ShurePlus MOTIV when a specific USB-C microphone is plugged in.

Soon after, I customised shortcuts for Adobe Audition's tools, settings, and panel configurations—some of which I quickly moved to the Logitech MX Master mouse for faster editing.

Taking It Further

This setup worked for a long time, until one day my 9to5Mac colleague Gui Rambo introduced me to a small macro keyboard he had purchased, featuring 12 keys and 3 knobs. I immediately became very interested and bought the same model.

Right out of the box, I found it required additional setup to work properly with macOS. Fortunately, a GitHub project handled all the complicated parts for me, and ChatGPT took care of the rest.

One benefit of this setup is having a dedicated keyboard to trigger Keyboard Maestro shortcuts, meaning I don't have to remember them, nor worry about ergonomic issues.

Additionally, because this keyboard can provide up to 3 layers with 12 keys per layer, and the knobs can also be pressed as buttons, I can use one mode of operation when working in Adobe Audition, and a completely different mode when working at the operating system level.

When working in Adobe Audition, this macro keyboard paired with the MX Master mouse allows me to quickly switch tools, export files (or just export selections), apply various effects such as volume normalisation, compression, de-reverb, de-essing, ripple delete, and more—orders of magnitude faster than using regular keyboard shortcuts, let alone not using shortcuts at all, and the workflow is much smoother.

At the operating system level, I can switch this same keyboard to another layer to just as easily switch audio input, adjust volume, fine-tune screen brightness, mute and unmute the microphone, and open frequently used folders.

Honestly, it took me a while to remember all these commands, but they became habits faster than I expected. More importantly, when I have to work in an environment without this setup, frankly, my Mac feels broken to me.

Furthermore, macro keyboards come in all sorts of configurations and options—shape, size, keys, knobs, lighting colours—you name it. There's really a sense of endless exploration in this area. If your work involves any repetitive actions (and whose doesn't?), I wholeheartedly recommend you try it for yourself.
